title: A Inventory for the Wardrobe
premise: Ivo Brightwater, a bridge inspector who measures everything in tolerances and load, has spent ten years in a marriage held together by what neither he nor his wife Maren says aloud. When contractors demolishing her childhood home find a box of undelivered letters behind the wardrobe — letters Ivo wrote to Maren before they married and never sent — the couple is forced to confront the decade of almost-speech that followed. Returning to the coastal town where their story first went wrong, they must decide whether love can survive being finally spoken before the house, and the last version of themselves, comes down. The novel ends not with reconciliation as erasure but with two people choosing each other with full knowledge of the cost.
about_author: Felix Pemberton is the pen name of a former structural engineer who spent fifteen years inspecting bridges along the northern coast before turning to fiction. His work examines the quiet mechanics of long relationships — the joints that flex, the ones that fail.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. On a routine bridge inspection, Ivo narrates his marriage through engineering metaphors: hairline cracks, acceptable deflection, loads borne without complaint. At home, Maren sets two plates at opposite ends of the table. The emotional beat is the ache of competence — a man who can diagnose any structure except his own life.

chapters.title: What the Wardrobe Kept
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. A call from the demolition contractor: workers found a tin box wired behind the wardrobe of her childhood bedroom. She opens it alone and finds forty-one unsent letters in Ivo's handwriting, dated the year before their wedding. The beat is vertigo — the past arriving with a return address she never gave it.

chapters.title: Forty-One Ways Not to Say It
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Confronted, Ivo admits he wrote the letters during their engagement and lost his nerve; when the house was sold, so was the box, or so he believed. Maren reads three aloud at the kitchen table, her voice flat as an inspector's report. The beat is exposure — ten years of practiced silence undone by paper.

chapters.title: The Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The house comes down in six weeks. Maren proposes returning to Saltmere Bay to sort through the rest of her mother's things, framing it as practicality. Ivo reads it correctly as an ultimatum dressed as logistics. The beat is negotiation between two people fluent in subtext and starved of plain speech.

chapters.title: Saltmere Bay
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. They arrive in the fading seaside town; the house smells of dust and brine. Old neighbors remember them as the couple who left too fast, twenty years ago, after something no one will name. The beat is the uncanny feeling of walking back into a room you fled.

chapters.title: The Summer of the Letters
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Sorting the attic, Ivo recalls why he never sent the letters: Maren's father had offered him the family business on the condition he stop 'dreaming on paper,' and Ivo chose security, then resented the choice daily. The beat is confession arriving sideways, through objects rather than words.

chapters.title: Her Mother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. In a locked drawer, Maren finds her mother's account book recording debts paid quietly for years — including money that kept Ivo's first business alive. Her parents knew about the letters all along and bought their silence. The beat is grief compounded: even her inheritance was a transaction.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A storm closes the coast road, stranding them in the half-emptied house. The argument ten years deferred finally breaks: duty versus love, the father's bargain, the child they didn't have, every unspoken thing at once. The beat is rupture — the structure failing exactly where it always flexed.

chapters.title: Load Test
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Morning after the storm, Ivo does the thing he has practiced for a decade: he says it plainly — that he chose wrongly, that he loved her in ink if not in voice, that he is asking for nothing. He mails one letter, forty-two years late, from the Saltmere post office. The beat is terrifying clarity.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. They watch the house come down together, holding the empty tin between them. Maren hands Ivo a letter of her own — written last night, unsent, given instead by hand. They drive home with the windows down. The beat is resolution without repair: not the marriage they planned, but one finally under real load, and holding.
